paras: The lynching of W. E. Graham took place on the night of January 2, 1882, when masked men took Graham from the jail at Ellsworth, Kansas, and hanged him from a telegraph pole. Graham was accused of killing and robbing his uncle, Philip Egley, at Venango in Ellsworth County and burning his house, and he was reported to have confessed in jail. The men went back for a second prisoner, W. C. Rose, but officers had already moved him. A brief wire dispatch carried the hanging to newspapers across the country, and the inquest verdict drew sarcastic comment as far away as Virginia.

On December 29, 1881, an Ellsworth dispatch reported that Philip Egley of Venango had been murdered the night before and his house burned, and that "the perpetrators of the deed are not known." Graham was soon jailed at Ellsworth; a Saline County Journal correspondent wrote that he had killed his uncle and fired his "shanty," "All for $125." J. C. Maltby of Wilson wrote that Graham told conflicting stories before confessing on the evening of January 2.

A later item from the Newport News of Pennsylvania said Graham was the son of Isaac Graham, a Newport blacksmith, and that Egley, also from Newport, had sold property and was killed for the money. In the cell next to Graham's was W. C. Rose, held for a double murder in the southeast part of the county the previous October.

According to the Saline County Journal's correspondent, who signed himself "B.," a party of masked horsemen rode quietly into Ellsworth at about 9 o'clock Monday evening, hitched their horses, and made for the jail. Sheriff Stebins met them there but was "powerless," and the men broke through doors and iron cells to reach Graham. They hurried him to the nearest telegraph pole, about 300 yards away, set a ladder against it, put a rope around his neck and told him to climb; at the fourth rung he "swung off."

The correspondent put the active participants at perhaps 25 and the witnesses at 300, and wrote that it had been "generally understood during the afternoon" that something of the kind would happen that night. Maltby, arriving in Ellsworth that night, saw Graham hanging from a telegraph pole in front of the jail and still "struggling in death."
The men then returned for Rose, but officers had got him away; the wire said the sheriff took him from the jail "during the excitement."

A coroner's jury found that Graham "came to his death from strangulation, in part from his own exertion, and by the hands of parties unknown"; since his arms had been pinioned, B. wrote, townspeople were divided over calling it suicide. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial of the lynchers appears in the coverage, which also does not show what became of Rose.

An Ellsworth dispatch dated January 3 ran the next day from Maine to Minnesota, headed "The Gailows [Gallows] Robbed of its Prey" in Portland, "Murderer Lynched in Kansas" in Richmond and "Kansas Lynching." in St. Paul. The dispatch described Graham as the man "who killed, robbed and burned Philip Egley," stating the accusation as fact, and placed the hanging "in front of the court house."

Weeklies reprinted the story into mid-January, the Millheim Journal of Pennsylvania under the headline "A Severe But Sure Cure" and the Gloucester County Democrat of New Jersey with the mob rendered as "a crowd." In Kansas the Saline County Journal printed two letters from Ellsworth, one headed "JUDGE LYNCH AT ELLSWORTH," and the Wichita City Eagle ran a version credited to a special to the Commonwealth. On February 18 the Stephens City Star of Virginia quoted the inquest verdict with the remark, "Very neat this, and characteristically Western."
None of the reports gave the race of Graham, Egley or Rose, and no Black-press coverage of the case was found.

Reports differ on where Graham died: the wire put the hanging in front of the court house, Maltby in front of the jail, and B., the most detailed eyewitness account, at a telegraph pole about 300 yards from the jail. The Wichita City Eagle dated the lynching Tuesday and named the prisoner "W. E. Chandler," though the same item later refers to "executing Graham."

bases: Masked men took Graham from the Ellsworth jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole for an alleged murder (A15, A14, A2).

Graham was hanged after being taken by force from the sheriff's jail by about 25 masked men, who acted on the accusation that he had murdered his uncle (A15, A14); every report calls the killers a mob (A2, A4).

The wire dispatch (A2, A4), two separate letters from Ellsworth to the Saline County Journal (A14, A15) and a Kansas special to the Commonwealth (A19) agree that a mob took Graham from the jail and hanged him.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Graham, who 'killed, robbed and burned' Egley, was hung by a mob in front of the court house; Rose was taken from the jail by the sheriff during the excitement.

accounts.label: Saline County Journal correspondent 'B.'
accounts.gist: About 25 masked horsemen overpowered Sheriff Stebins, broke into the cells, and hanged the confessed murderer from a telegraph pole 300 yards from the jail before 300 witnesses; officers had removed Rose before they returned.

accounts.label: J. C. Maltby of Wilson
accounts.gist: Graham confessed that evening after telling conflicting stories; the mob took him from the jail and hung him to a telegraph pole in front of the jail, then went back for Rose, who at 11 o'clock had not been hanged.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death from strangulation, 'in part from his own exertion, and by the hands of parties unknown.'

accounts.label: Special to the Commonwealth
accounts.gist: On Tuesday a prisoner named 'W. E. Chandler,' held for the Egley killing, was taken from the jail by a mob and hung in front of the courthouse; Rose was taken to safety by the sheriff.

accounts.label: Newport (Pa.) News
accounts.gist: Graham, son of a Newport blacksmith, killed his uncle Egly, also from Newport, for money from a property sale and set the house on fire.

framing.detail: The wire dispatch ran under headlines such as 'The Gailows Robbed of its Prey' (Portland), 'Murderer Lynched in Kansas' (Richmond) and 'Kansas Lynching.' (St. Paul), stating the accusation as fact.
The Millheim Journal printed the wire dispatch under the headline 'A Severe But Sure Cure.'
The Saline County Journal ran its correspondent's letter as 'JUDGE LYNCH AT ELLSWORTH,' describing the 'confessed murderer' and remarking dryly on the inquest verdict.
The Stephens City Star quoted the inquest verdict as 'Very neat this, and characteristically Western,' mocking it without comment on the lynching itself.

conflicts.note: The two Ellsworth letters (A14, A15) were written by men on the scene; B.'s letter gives the most detail.
Maltby's letter is dated January 2 and describes the hanging that evening; the Wichita item's 'Tuesday' is a single, secondhand version.
The Wichita item itself later refers to 'executing Graham,' so 'Chandler' appears to be an error.
